name: dao-factory
intent: Hand out a coherent family of data access objects bound to the store this deployment actually runs on: one factory object per store (the Factory Method form when there is a single store, the Abstract Factory form when stores vary) owns driver, dialect, connection and pooling policy, so the store choice is made once at the composition root and business components never name a vendor.
problem: The persistence technology is not fixed: development runs on SQLite or H2, production on PostgreSQL or Oracle, one customer keeps a legacy system behind a service, tests want an in-memory store. Yet every business component constructs its own DAOs, so each one hard-codes a driver, a dialect, a connection policy and often a store key. Changing or adding a store then means editing business code in many places, and nothing prevents two components from silently talking to two different stores.
context: Persistence layers where the store implementation varies per deployment, per customer or per environment (relational vendors, embedded databases, files, remote services) and where clients must stay independent of the vendor API. It applies when DAO interfaces exist or can be defined cleanly, when the store choice can be made once per application, tenant or session at a composition root or onboarding step, and - in the Factory Method form - when a single store merely needs one place to construct its DAOs. Where a dependency-injection container, an ORM dialect layer or a provider factory already resolves implementations from configuration, that mechanism is the factory and a hand-written hierarchy only adds a second composition root.
benefits: Store knowledge is confined to the concrete factories and their DAOs: business code compiles against DAO interfaces only, so moving a deployment to another vendor is a new concrete factory plus a configuration change, not an edit in every component.
The store choice is made exactly once and consistently: one factory instance serves the application (or tenant), so two components cannot accidentally talk to two different stores or dialects.
New stores plug in without touching clients (open/closed on the store axis): a concrete factory and its DAO family are added, and the selection table gains one entry.
Testing gets a real seam: swapping in an in-memory or fake factory family exercises whole application flows without a database, and each store's family can be contract-tested against its own backend.

Resource and security policy centralise: driver registration, connection-string and credential resolution, pooling and dialect setup live in the factory instead of being scattered (or duplicated) across DAO constructors.
Cross-DAO invariants hold: DAOs handed out by one factory share the same store, schema version and transaction context, which is what makes a Unit of Work over several DAOs coherent.
tradeoffs: One more layer and a hierarchy to design: an abstract factory plus one concrete factory per store (and one DAO interface per entity). With a single store and no second one on the roadmap this is pure ceremony - the catalog itself advises starting with the Factory Method form and escalating to per-store abstract factories only when the store actually varies.

The DAO-kind axis is rigid: adding one entity to the persistence layer means extending the abstract factory and every concrete factory - the classic Abstract Factory cost, paid on the axis teams change most often (entities), not the one the pattern protects (stores).

The store choice becomes invisible at call sites, which helps while it works and hurts when it does not: a missing or misconfigured entry is discovered at runtime (possibly on the first request that touches it) instead of at compile time, and a failure may originate in the selection table, the factory, the DAO or the driver.

Configuration and lifetime become part of the design: the factory holds connection configuration and often a pool, so a stale factory instance pins a stale endpoint or credential, while global factory singletons with setters create mutable global state that breaks test isolation and races between tenants.

The migration benefit is only as good as interface purity: DAO methods that expose vendor types (ResultSet, DbDataReader, OCI handles) or baked-in dialect assumptions let the factory be swapped without migrating the application, giving a false sense of portability.

In container-based stacks the pattern competes with the composition root: a hand-written DAO factory next to container registration duplicates the selection logic and leaves two places that decide which store is active.

participants.responsibility: The business or presentation component that needs data; it obtains DAOs from the factory and works only through the DAO interfaces - it never names a concrete store, driver or SQL dialect.
The abstract creator: declares one creation operation per DAO kind (getCustomerDAO(), orderDao()) or a single typed lookup; it is the only creation interface clients depend on.

One implementation per store or vendor: knows driver, connection string, dialect, schema and pooling policy, instantiates the matching concrete DAOs, and is the only place where the store API names appear.
Abstract product per entity or aggregate: the store-agnostic persistence operations (find, insert, update, delete, query) that every store family must provide.
The store-specific implementation of a DAO: SQL or store API calls, result-to-record mapping, dialect quirks and error translation live here, hidden behind the DAO interface.
The actual backend the factory configures and injects into the concrete DAOs - a pool, a connection, a client, a session; its lifecycle is part of the factory's contract.
The data carrier crossing the DAO boundary (DTO, record, struct, Row): it keeps DAO signatures free of vendor types and is what allows every store family to implement the same interface.

use_cases: Multi-database deployments: one application runs on SQLite or H2 in development and PostgreSQL or Oracle in production, and the factory reads the active store from configuration.
Vendor-portable products: an ISV hands the same DAO interfaces to customers running SQL Server, PostgreSQL or Oracle, with one concrete factory family per supported store.
Test infrastructure: a fake or in-memory factory family is bound in tests while the real factory is bound in production, so application flows run without a database.

Multi-tenant SaaS: the factory resolves the tenant's store (its schema, database or shard) and hands out DAOs bound to that tenant's connection. Tenant-scoped factory families prevent cross-tenant data leakage by ensuring every DAO query carries the tenant context from the factory's connection or session state.
Legacy and cloud coexistence during migration: two factory families stand behind one DAO interface set, letting reads and writes move store by store instead of in one big-bang cutover.

Pluggable backends: DAOs contributed by plugins or optional modules (a JDBC driver JAR, a ServiceLoader provider, a Python entry-point package) are resolved at startup by store key without recompiling the application.

Runtime data source selection: the factory selects the active data source at startup or request time based on environment variables, feature flags or feature flags, enabling blue-green deployments where different store families are active for different traffic shares.

ORM-backed persistence with portable interfaces: when using JPA/Hibernate, wrap EntityManagerFactory or SessionFactory behind a DAO factory interface so that the domain layer stays independent of the ORM provider and unit tests can substitute a lightweight in-memory implementation.

Microservices with per-service data stores: each microservice owns its data store; the service's DAO factory hides whether that store is PostgreSQL, MongoDB or a proprietary external service, and the factory interface becomes the integration contract for that service's data domain.

A/B testing with different storage backends: a feature flag routes traffic to one of several concrete factory families (e.g., legacy v2 vs. new v3 store), enabling gradual rollout and canary testing of a new database technology without changing any DAO interface.

ADO.NET provider factory: System.Data.Common's DbProviderFactory is the framework's own Abstract Factory - DbProviderFactories.GetFactory(invariantName) returns the registered SqlClientFactory or Npgsql factory and creates provider-specific Connection, Command and DataAdapter objects from a config-supplied provider name, which is exactly the store-selection machinery a hand-written DAO factory duplicates.

JDBC DataSource: javax.sql.DataSource is a vendor-implemented factory for connections; bound to a JNDI logical name (jdbc/sampledb) the application asks for a logical resource instead of naming a driver class or URL, and swapping the database vendor becomes a deployment change - the Java platform's built-in version of the DAO factory seam.

Spring Boot DataSourceBuilder: Boot reads spring.datasource.url, infers the driver and pooling implementation from the classpath and builds a HikariDataSource or vendor DataSource; here the framework is the factory, so the DAO layer consumes the built DataSource rather than re-deciding the store in a parallel hand-written hierarchy.
avoid_when: There is one store and no realistic second one: construct the DAO directly, or use a single Factory-Method-style creator for that store; escalate to per-store abstract factories only when the store actually changes.

A dependency-injection container already binds implementations: register the store-specific DAOs per profile or key (.NET keyed services, Spring profiles and qualifiers, CDI alternatives, NestJS providers) instead of hand-writing a parallel factory.

A driver, ORM or query builder already implements store-neutral access: create_engine('postgresql+psycopg://...'), Sequel.connect('postgres://...'), DbProviderFactories.GetFactory(...) or sqlx::Any resolve the store from a URL or provider name, so wrap that in the DAO layer instead of building a second selection mechanism.
The DAO surface is one or two entities with stable operations: a Table Data Gateway module, a Repository or plain driver calls are simpler, and the extra factory hierarchy never pays back.

Store selection must happen per call rather than per application (sharding by key, read/write splitting per query, routing by request): that is a routing decision inside the data-access layer, not a creation-time factory.
anti_patterns: A factory that returns concrete store types: clients downcast, type-check or compare DAO classes (or reach for the driver through the DAO), so the abstraction is bypassed and every new store breaks callers.

Global mutable factory: a static or singleton factory with a setter used to switch stores at runtime - hidden global state that tests leak into each other and that multi-tenant or concurrent contexts race on.
Factory lookup on the hot path: calling the selection function inside loops or per repository call, turning a composition-root decision into per-operation overhead and noise.

A factory per DAO kind, or one concrete factory class with a switch in every method: the class explosion the pattern was meant to tame, with the store and DAO-kind axes crossed in hand-written branches.

Leaky DAO interfaces: methods typed in vendor terms (ResultSet, DbDataReader, OCI handles, dialect-specific SQL strings in signatures) that make the family unimplementable by another store while the factory pretends portability.

Two composition roots: a hand-written DAOFactory duplicating what container registration, ServiceLoader, entry points or the ORM dialect registry already resolve, so the active store can be decided in two different places.
pitfalls: Connection pool misconfiguration per tenant: a factory that initialises a connection pool at startup and never recreates it will serve stale credentials or endpoints if tenant configuration changes at runtime. Pools must be invalidated and recreated on configuration change, or the factory must be reconstructed.

Dialect escaping differences across stores: identical-looking SQL strings behave differently across vendors (quote character, NULL handling in UNIQUE, string concatenation operator). A DAO that compiles SQL as a constant and passes it unchanged to two store families will silently produce wrong results or errors on one of them.

Schema version skew between store families: two concrete factory families for the same logical schema may drift if migration scripts are not applied uniformly. A DAO family that works against schema v2 of one store may issue queries incompatible with schema v1 of another.

Lazy factory initialisation and first-request latency: deferring store resolution or connection acquisition to the first DAO call adds unpredictable latency to that request and surfaces configuration errors late. Resolve and validate the store at startup.

Thread safety in factory caching: a factory that caches DAO instances in a shared mutable map without synchronisation will leak instances between request contexts in a concurrent server. Cache DAOs per request scope or per thread, not in a shared unguarded map.

Swallowing store-specific exceptions in concrete DAOs: translating vendor exceptions to a common type is correct, but translating them to a generic RuntimeException or logging and returning null erases the cause and makes debugging across store families very difficult.

Per-tenant factory without schema isolation verification: creating a per-tenant factory that shares a schema (multi-tenant shared schema) does not automatically add tenant filtering - the factory must inject tenant context into every query, and tests must verify that context is not lost on eager-loaded relations.

Mismatched transaction boundaries across DAOs: if each DAO independently opens and commits its own transaction, a Unit of Work that spans multiple DAOs will not be atomic. The factory should propagate a shared transaction context (connection, session, Unit of Work reference) to all DAOs it creates.
Returning concrete types from factory methods: exposing concrete DAO classes forces clients to depend on vendor types and defeats the abstraction. Always return interfaces or abstract classes.

Hardcoding store keys in multiple locations: if the active store key appears in both the factory registry and in DAO constructors, the two can diverge silently. Keep the store key in one place (configuration) and derive all factory behaviour from it.

Mixing data-source selection with DAO creation: a factory that also implements query routing (read/write split, shard routing) mixes two responsibilities. Keep the factory as a creation seam and handle routing inside the DAO layer.

Forgetting to close resources in concrete DAOs: a concrete DAO that opens connections, statements or result sets without proper try/finally or language-level resource management will leak connections, especially under pooling.

Using DAO interfaces that expose scrollable cursors or vendor-specific query objects: these types leak store knowledge into the client and make swapping the factory family impossible without client changes.

Assuming store order in results: SQL does not guarantee row order without ORDER BY. A DAO that returns results assuming a particular order (first row, last row) and works on one store may fail on another that returns rows differently.

Wrong move: hand-write a DAO factory hierarchy next to a mechanism that already resolves the store from configuration (Spring profiles and DataSourceBuilder, .NET keyed services, DbProviderFactories) -> two composition roots decide which store is active and silently drift apart -> instead: designate the framework's factory or registration as the single selection point and keep only the DAO interfaces hand-written.

Wrong move: build the abstract factory plus per-store DAO families while only one store exists and no second is scheduled -> interfaces with a single implementation, factory methods for every entity and a removal cost far above the concrete class they wrapped -> instead: start with concrete DAOs and introduce the factory axis only when a second store is real and dated.

Wrong move: let DAO signatures pass vendor types (IQueryable, ResultSet, live ORM sessions) because store-neutral mapping is tedious -> the factory can be swapped but no second family can actually implement the interface, and the mocked tests built on it stay brittle -> instead: materialise results to DTOs or records inside the concrete DAO, or, if a mature ORM is the only store, use it directly in the infrastructure layer instead of a fake-neutral factory.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: clients depend on DAO interfaces and on the factory abstraction, never on driver classes or concrete DAOs.
Single responsibility: deciding and configuring the store (factory) is separate from executing persistence operations (DAO).
Open/closed on the store axis: new stores arrive as new concrete factories and DAO families without editing clients.
Program to an interface, not an implementation: the store API names stay inside the concrete factory and the concrete DAO.
Encapsulate what varies: the varying dimension is the store or vendor, captured once in the factory while DAO interfaces stay stable.
best_practices: Decide the store once, at the composition root (main, DI registration, configuration loader, tenant onboarding) and inject the factory or the DAOs; never let business code resolve a store key for itself.
Keep DAO interfaces store-agnostic - domain and record types only - and let concrete DAOs translate vendor errors into a common error vocabulary.

Make the factory immutable and explicit about lifetime: one instance per store (or per tenant) per process, created with its configuration and never switched afterwards; prefer constructor injection over static setters.
Fail fast on an unknown store key with a clear message, and validate at startup (open the store, check the schema version) rather than on first use.
Provide a fake or in-memory factory family for tests, and keep a contract test battery that every concrete DAO family must pass - it is the real guarantee that the families are interchangeable.
Leave transaction boundaries in the client (Unit of Work or explicit commit) and pooling/credential handling in the factory; DAOs must not commit on their own.
Start with the Factory Method shape for a single store and create per-store abstract factories only when a second store is actually scheduled.
Bind the factory to the request or tenant scope, not to a static or singleton lifetime, so that concurrent requests or tenants cannot observe each other's store configuration.

Write integration tests that spin up the actual store (or a dockerised equivalent) for every concrete DAO family and run the full contract test battery against it; unit tests alone cannot validate SQL dialect compatibility.
Keep the factory registry in one central place (one module, one configuration file) so that auditing which store is active requires reading one location, not grepping the codebase.
Use a common exception hierarchy for DAO errors and translate store-specific exceptions in concrete DAOs; never let vendor exceptions propagate to clients.
Version the DAO interface contract independently from concrete implementations; breaking changes to the interface require a migration path, not just a new factory family.
When the DAO interface is stable and the store is not, prefer injecting the DAO (not the factory) so that the factory is resolved only at the composition root.
Cache DAO instances per request or session scope, not globally; a shared mutable cache without synchronization leaks instances across concurrent contexts.
When using an ORM, treat the EntityManagerFactory or SessionFactory as the factory and DAO interfaces as the abstraction layer on top, rather than duplicating the factory pattern below the ORM.

related_patterns_notes.data-access-object: The base pattern whose creation the DAO Factory automates. DAO defines the abstract persistence interface (find, insert, update, delete) that all concrete DAOs implement; the factory is the creation mechanism for those products.
related_patterns_notes.abstract-factory: The structural pattern DAO Factory implements. Abstract Factory creates families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes; DAO Factory applies this to create a family of store-specific DAOs (CustomerDAO, OrderDAO, etc.) from one concrete factory per backend. The GoF book (Gamma et al., 1994) defines the structure and tradeoffs.
related_patterns_notes.factory-method: The simpler creation pattern DAO Factory falls back to when only one store exists. A single factory method per DAO kind is sufficient; the per-store abstract factory is added only when the store axis actually varies. GoF Factory Method is used inside each concrete DAO factory to instantiate individual DAOs.
related_patterns_notes.registry: The DAO Factory often uses a registry (map or dictionary) keyed by store identifier to hold the concrete factory constructors or instances. The registry is the selection table that maps 'postgresql', 'oracle', 'sqlite' to their respective factory classes. Fowler's Registry pattern provides the well-known lookup mechanism used here.
related_patterns_notes.dependency-injection: The composition root that typically supplies the DAO Factory to clients. A DI container holds the factory instance (or its configuration) and injects it into business components, making the factory itself a dependency like any other. Inverting factory construction to the container avoids a hand-written factory locator.
related_patterns_notes.repository: Often compared with DAO but at a higher level of domain abstraction. A Repository presents a collection-like interface to domain objects and typically delegates to DAOs internally. The DAO Factory can create the DAOs that a Repository implementation depends on, but the Repository itself adds domain-centric query composition on top. Fowler (2002) defines Repository as mediating between domain and data mapping layers.
related_patterns_notes.table-data-gateway: A simpler alternative when the DAO surface is one table or view. Table Data Gateway holds all SQL for one table and is instantiated per table; DAO Factory becomes unnecessary ceremony when there is only one entity and one store. When the entity count grows or multiple stores appear, Table Data Gateway instances are created by the DAO Factory.
related_patterns_notes.data-mapper: The layer that moves data between domain objects and the database, often used inside a ConcreteDAO implementation. A Data Mapper handles the object-table translation while the DAO delegates to it; the DAO Factory creates the mappers along with the DAO or the mapper is created by the DAO itself. Fowler (2002) defines Data Mapper as an O/RM structural pattern.
related_patterns_notes.unit-of-work: Tracks dirty, new and deleted objects within a business transaction and commits them atomically. DAOs produced by a DAO Factory share the same store and typically participate in a shared Unit of Work scope, since the factory ensures all DAOs in a session use the same connection or transaction context. Fowler (2002) defines Unit of Work as coordinating writes and concurrency.
related_patterns_notes.identity-map: Ensures each database row is loaded only once, keeping tracked objects in a map by primary key. Often used alongside DAO and Unit of Work to avoid duplicate queries within a session; the identity map's scope is tied to the DAO or Unit of Work scope that the factory establishes. Fowler (2002) defines Identity Map as preventing duplicate loading.
related_patterns_notes.active-record: An object that wraps a database row and adds domain logic. When using Active Record (e.g., Rails, Django ORM), the DAO factory concept shifts: the factory creates Active Record instances rather than pure DAOs, and the 'factory' is often implicit in the ORM's model base class. The DAO Factory pattern is still relevant when wrapping an ORM behind a clean persistence interface.
related_patterns_notes.gateway: An object that encapsulates access to an external system or resource. A concrete DAO is often a Gateway to the database. DAO Factory can be seen as a factory that produces families of Gateways for different store backends. Fowler (2002) defines Gateway as encapsulating all access to an external system.
